Data visualization guide

How McKesson Workforce Innovation turns workforce data into charts that lead to decisions.

Version 0.2 (pilot)September 2026All example data is synthetic
McKesson Data Visualization GuideOverview1

Overview

How to use this guide

One set of rules, three ways in. The guide teaches the thinking; the starter kit makes the right answer the easy one in every tool we use.

Every chart we make should do one job: answer a business question so clearly that the reader knows what to do next. The rules here are written to be checked, by a reviewer or by an agent, before a chart leaves the team.

Inspired by the structure of a leading consulting firm's public data-visualization guide, rebuilt for McKesson's brand and for the work of Workforce Innovation.

Consultants and analysts

Decks, reports, workbooks

Read Fundamentals once, then use the chart pages as you build. Keep the cheat sheet next to you.

  • PowerPoint template and starter deck
  • Excel chart workbook with the palette
  • One-page cheat sheet and chart chooser
  • Power BI report theme

Developers and data scientists

Python, HTML, R, Power BI

Each chart page links to tested code. Themes are generated from one token file, so every tool matches.

  • mckviz for matplotlib and Plotly
  • CSS variables, Plotly and Vega-Lite themes
  • theme_mck() for ggplot2
  • mv.lint(fig) to check a chart

Coding agents

Claude, Copilot and others

Agents read AGENTS.md automatically in this repo. For other repos, copy one self-contained rules file.

  • AGENTS.md: workflow and rules
  • mck-chart skill: question to QA
  • dist/agents/mck-viz-rules.md
  • Cookbook pages with runnable snippets

The five steps behind every chart

1 Question. Write the question the chart answers in one sentence.

2 Chart. Pick the chart from the question type, not from habit.

3 Build. Grey first, then color only what the headline names.

4 Headline. Compute the finding, then write it as a sentence.

5 QA. Run the checklist and look at the rendered chart.

Fundamentals

Start with the question, not the chart

A chart is finished when a reader can say what it means and what to do about it, without you in the room.

Before you open a tool, write the question in one sentence: "Where is attrition concentrated?", not "show attrition".

Then pick the mode. Explanatory charts prove a finding, for decks and reports (the default). Exploratory views let readers find answers, for dashboards. Both follow the same rules.

Both charts here are accurate; only one is useful in a meeting.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals4

Fundamentals

How readers read a chart

Readers move through a chart in three steps. Design for each one, in order.

1 Perceive

In the first second the eye takes in shape, length and color before reading a word. Make the thing that matters the thing that stands out: one color against grey.

2 Interpret

Next the reader looks for meaning: headline, labels, units, benchmarks. The headline should confirm what they just saw, or sharpen it.

3 Act

Finally they ask "so what?". A callout that sizes the implication turns a finding into a decision.

Step 1 · Perceive

Two bars stand out

No words yet. Grey context and blue focus already tell the reader where to look.

Step 2 · Interpret

Labels give it meaning

Names, values and a labelled benchmark show the two families sit well above 19.9%.

Step 3 · Act

The callout sizes the prize

Together they hold 58% of headcount but 73% of voluntary exits: a retention plan for two families moves the enterprise number.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals5

Fundamentals

Anatomy of a chart

Every McKesson chart has the same four layers, top to bottom: headline, subtitle, chart, and footnote with source.

The headline and subtitle do different jobs. The headline is editorial: it states the finding. The subtitle is neutral: metric, unit, scope and period.

Inside the chart, everything is labelled in place, so the reader never has to match colors to a legend.

All four layers share one left edge. In HTML they are page text; the chart library draws only the data.

  1. 1Insight headlineA full sentence with the number. At most two lines, no final period.
  2. 2SubtitleMetric, unit, scope and period. No opinions.
  3. 3Direct labelsSeries named at the line end, in the series color. No legend.
  4. 4Focus and contextThe series the headline is about is blue; the comparison is grey.
  5. 5Forecast markedA shaded period and dashed lines separate estimates from actuals.
  6. 6Range, not a pointForecasts show their uncertainty.
  7. 7The point, annotatedThe gap the headline quotes, labelled where it is.
  8. 8Light scaffoldingFew, light gridlines; units live in the subtitle.
  9. 9Footnote and sourceDefinitions, system, as-of date, population.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals6

Fundamentals

Write the headline last, from the numbers

The headline is the most-read text on the page. It should be the finding, not the topic.

The formula

Who or what + verb + number + so what.

Before you keep it

  • Recompute every number, "all", "most" and "n of m" from the data
  • The blue in the chart is what the headline names
  • Two lines at most; no final period

If you can't write a headline, you don't have a finding yet: you have a chart.

Label
Attrition by job family · names the topic; says nothing
Vague
Attrition varies across job families · true of every chart ever made
Opinion
Attrition is out of control in the frontline · a claim the chart can't support
Insight
Two frontline job families lose about 1 in 4 people a year, well above the 19.9% enterprise rate
Insight + action
Two frontline families account for 73% of voluntary exits; retention there moves the enterprise rate
McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals7

Fundamentals

Grey first, then color the point

Color is for meaning, never decoration. Start with every mark in grey, then color only what the headline names.

Highlight at most two items. When everything is highlighted, nothing is.

Echo the highlight in the text: bold the matching category label, and set callouts in the color of the mark they describe.

Orange means "worse". Keep it for negatives: below target, shrinking, a shortfall. Never use it as a plain highlight; readers take it as a warning.

Pattern 1 · Default

Focus

All grey; the items the headline names in blue.

Pattern 2

Uniform + accent

One series in light blue; the single exception in navy.

Pattern 3

Focus + accent

Grey context, a blue group, one navy exception. Use sparingly.

Color roles

Context · everything the reader should see but not focus on#B4B0A5
Focus · what the headline names#005A8C
Accent · the one exception that must pop (navy, not orange)#143359
Light blue · the series when navy marks the exception#66C4FF
Orange · only when it means worse: below target, shrinking, a shortfall#EF8200
Total and benchmark · totals, targets, reference lines#143359
Context light · de-emphasized fills in stacks and areas#DEDBD1
McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals8

Fundamentals

Three palettes, three jobs

Pick the palette from what the color encodes.

Categories

Only when categories must be told apart. At most six, always in the same order, so "Full-time" is the same blue on every slide.

One measure, light to dark

For heat tables and choropleths of a single measure. Darker means more.

Gap to a benchmark

For values centered on zero or a target. Orange below, blue above, a neutral middle.

Text on a fill switches between white and navy, whichever contrasts more (mv.text_on).

Categorical

Voluntary attrition, FY26 (%)

Diverging

McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals9

Fundamentals

Type and proportion

One typeface, Libre Franklin, in a few fixed roles. Type should frame the data, not compete with it.

The headline is the largest text on the chart but the data is the largest thing. If the headline is the first thing you notice from across the room, it is too heavy.

  • Nothing below 9 pt on slides, 11 px on screens
  • Sentence case everywhere; no all-caps headlines
  • Headline, subtitle, key, footnote and source share one left edge
  • Big numbers use the light weight

Libre Franklin is open source (SIL OFL). Set-up for Office, the web and Power BI is in the Toolkit.

RoleSampleWeightSlideScreen
HeadlineAttrition is concentrated in two job familiesBold24 pt22 px
SubtitleVoluntary attrition, FY26 (%)Regular14 pt15 px
Data labels27.4%Medium12 pt13 px
Axis and category labelsPharmacy TechnicianRegular11 pt12 px
CalloutsHiring freeze, Q2Regular12 pt13 px
Footnote and sourceSource: Workday HCM, as of 31 Mar 2026Light9 pt11 px
Big number75%Light54 pt56 px

Proportion on a 16:9 slide

Margins of about 0.5 in. The chart takes at least 60% of the slide height. One message per chart, at most two charts per slide; the slide title is the headline.

Proportion on a screen

The chart card sits on a quiet background with generous padding. Headline about 1.4× the subtitle. On phones, swap end labels for a top key and let wide exhibits scroll sideways rather than shrink.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals10

Fundamentals

Label directly, delete the rest

Every element must earn its place. If removing it loses nothing, remove it.

  1. Replace the label-style title with an insight headline
  2. Sort by value, not alphabet
  3. Turn long-named columns into horizontal bars
  4. Grey everything, then color the point
  5. Label values in place; delete the value axis, gridlines and tick marks
  6. Delete the legend, borders and background fill
  7. Add the benchmark, labelled where it sits
McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals11

Fundamentals

Honest scales

A chart can be accurate in every number and still mislead. These four rules prevent the common ways.

Bars start at zero. If the differences only show on a narrow range, change the chart, not the axis.

No dual axes. Two scales let you make any two lines cross wherever you like.

Bubble area, not diameter, is proportional to value.

Pies take five slices at most, and sum to 100%.

The one exception: a waterfall bridging two large totals may break its axis, if the break is drawn and footnoted.

Truncated bars

✕Try to avoidAn axis from 65 turns a 4% difference into a 33% one.
✓RecommendedA dot plot compares position, so the range can be narrow.

Dual axes

✕Try to avoidThe crossing point is an artifact of two chosen scales.
✓RecommendedTwo aligned charts share the time axis.

Bubble size

✕Try to avoidSized by diameter, 900 looks 81× bigger than 100.
✓RecommendedSized by area, 900 is 9× bigger, as it should be.

Too many slices

✕Try to avoidEight similar angles can't be ranked by eye.
✓RecommendedA sorted bar ranks them instantly.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals12

Fundamentals

People data is personal

Workforce charts describe colleagues, and carry extra obligations.

Minimum group size

No group under 10 people: not in bars, labels, tooltips, filters or drill-downs. Merge into "Other" and footnote it.

No re-identification

Small team × tenure × location can single out one person, even when each cut is large.

Protected attributes and forecasts

Protected attributes only for approved analyses such as pay equity, aggregated. Label estimates and show a range. Frame findings about roles, not individuals.

Engagement by team, one distribution center

Two teams have fewer than 10 respondents: anyone who knows the team can guess who answered what.

TeamRespondentsEngagement
Inbound4671
Outbound3868
Returns752
Quality488
Site leadership981
✕Try to avoidReporting groups below the minimum, even in a table or tooltip.

Engagement by team, one distribution center

Small teams combined into one group that clears the threshold.

TeamRespondentsEngagement
Inbound4671
Outbound3868
Other teams (3 combined)2072
✓RecommendedMerge into "Other" and footnote it: "Teams with fewer than 10 respondents are combined."

In dashboards, enforce it in the data model

A rule in a slide is easy to forget; a rule in the measure can't be skipped. In Power BI: IF([Headcount] < 10, BLANK(), [Engagement]). In Python, drop or merge small groups before plotting, and keep individual values out of hover text.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals13

Fundamentals

Accessible by default

About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have a color-vision deficiency. In a room of 25, assume someone does.

  • Text contrast at least 4.5:1
  • Never red vs. green; use blues and navy, with orange only for "worse"
  • Never color alone: pair it with labels, position or shape
  • Nothing below 9 pt on slides or 11 px on screens
  • Alt text for every chart that leaves the team: the headline plus two or three key numbers

The red–green examples are simulated for deuteranopia, the most common form.

Red vs. green

✕As seen with deuteranopiaRed and green hires vs. exits become one color.
✓As seen with deuteranopiaBlue and light blue stay distinct.

Color as the only cue

✕Try to avoidThe reader matches colors to a legend.
✓RecommendedNames at the line ends; color only reinforces.

Text on fills

✕Try to avoidWhite on every fill fails on the light ones.
✓RecommendedWhite or navy, whichever contrasts more.

Alt text

Write it from the headline and the numbers that prove it.

Alt: Two frontline job families lose about 1 in 4 people a year, well above the 19.9% enterprise rate. Pharmacy Technician 27.4%; Distribution Center Associate 24.1%; all other job families are below the enterprise rate.

In PowerPoint: right-click the chart, View Alt Text. In HTML: aria-label on the figure.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideFundamentals14

Magnitude

Bar chart

Magnitude charts compare size: which is bigger (relative), and by how much (absolute).

A bar's length is proportional to its value, so bars are the most precise way to compare categories. Sorted horizontal bars are the default for ranking job families, sites or skills: long names stay readable, and the layout works on a phone.

Use columns for a few time periods or short names.

McKesson spec

  • Bar about 2× the gap (Excel gap width 50%)
  • Sorted by value unless there's a natural order
  • Up to about 12 bars; group the tail into "Other"
  • No group under 10 people
  1. 1Insight headlineNames the two families and the benchmark they beat.
  2. 2SubtitleMetric, unit, scope, period.
  3. 3Focus in blueOnly the bars the headline names; two at most.
  4. 4Echo in the labelFocus categories in bold navy.
  5. 5Values on the barsSo the value axis and gridlines go.
  6. 6Labelled benchmarkA thin dashed line, named where it sits.
  7. 7Zero baselineA thin axis line; bars always start at zero.
  8. 8Grey contextEverything else, sorted by value.
  9. 9Footnote and sourceDefines the metric; names system, date, population.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideMagnitude15

Magnitude

Bar chart variants

Same rules, different shapes. Pick the variant from the comparison you need to make.

When a bar is the wrong chart

  • Values bunched far from zero (engagement 71–78): use a dot plot
  • Largest more than 20× the smallest: use proportional bubbles or split the chart
  • Parts of a whole: use a 100% stacked bar or waterfall
  • Many periods: use a line
  • Spread across people: use a distribution

Column chart

A few periods in time order, or short category names. Here internal fill rose from 22% to 29%.

Grouped bars

Two or three series per category. Prior period in light grey, current in blue; key top-left.

Diverging bars

Values on both sides of zero. Three job families shrank in FY26 despite hiring; negatives in orange.

Butterfly chart

Two measures back to back on the same items: FY26 exits and hires by job family.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideMagnitude16

Magnitude

Bar chart best practice

Four rules that fix most bar charts.

Size of bars. Thin bars pull the eye to the empty space between them. Make each bar about twice as wide as the gap.

Color of bars. A different color per bar distracts and implies categories that don't exist. One color; shade only the highlight.

Direct labels. Gridlines and a value axis add noise. Label the bars and delete both.

Zero baseline. Bar length encodes quantity, so never truncate. If the data needs a narrow range, switch to a line or dot plot.

Size of bars

✕Try to avoidStick-thin bars; the gaps dominate.
✓RecommendedBar about twice the gap.

Color of bars

✕Try to avoidA color per bar, encoding nothing.
✓RecommendedGrey bars; blue for the one that matters.

Direct labels

✕Try to avoidGridlines and an axis to read values from.
✓RecommendedValues on the bars; no axis, no grid.

Zero baseline

✕Try to avoidA truncated axis exaggerates differences.
✓RecommendedA line or dot plot can use a narrow range.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideMagnitude17

Magnitude

Bar chart best practice, continued

Four more, from reviewing workforce decks.

Sort with intent. Alphabetical order hides the ranking. Sort by value unless the categories have a natural order: tenure bands, job levels, survey scales.

Horizontal for long names. Rotated labels are slow to read. Job-family names need horizontal bars.

Label the benchmark in place. A reference line explained in a legend makes the reader search. Name it on the line.

Two highlights at most. Five colored bars in two colors is decoration, not emphasis.

Sort with intent

✕Try to avoidAlphabetical: the ranking is hidden.
✓RecommendedBy value, largest on top.

Horizontal for long names

✕Try to avoidTilted names the reader has to decode.
✓RecommendedHorizontal bars; names read naturally.

Label the benchmark

✕Try to avoidA legend for one line, in a highlight color.
✓RecommendedNavy dashed line, named on the line.

Two highlights at most

✕Try to avoidEverything highlighted means nothing is.
✓RecommendedThe two the headline names.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideMagnitude18

Magnitude

Build a bar chart

The same chart in every tool we use. Each recipe starts from the starter kit, so the colors and fonts are already right.

Full, tested code for each platform is on the cookbook page: docs/cookbook/bar.md.

Before you send it

  • Starts at zero; bar about 2× the gap
  • Sorted by value or a natural order
  • Values labelled; no value axis or gridlines
  • At most two highlights, matching the headline
  • Benchmark labelled in place
  • No group under 10 people
PowerPoint and Excel

Start from the starter deck or chart workbook in dist/office/. Insert a clustered bar, sort the data ascending (so the largest is on top), set Gap Width 50%, fill all bars with Context grey and the focus bars with Focus blue. Add data labels at Outside End; delete the value axis, gridlines, legend and chart title. The slide title is the headline.

Power BI

Import mckesson-dataviz-theme.json and sort the bars by the measure. Drive the highlight from a measure, not by clicking bars: a Bar color measure returns the focus blue when attrition is above 20% and context grey otherwise, applied through Colors › fx › Field value. Turn on data labels; turn off the X axis and gridlines. See docs/powerbi-setup.md.

Python

matplotlib with mckviz; Plotly uses the same helpers (mv.pl_highlight).

bars = ax.barh(df.job_family, df.rate, height=0.67,
               color=mv.highlight(df.job_family, focus=focus))
mv.label_bars(ax, bars, fmt="{:.1f}%")
mv.clean_axes(ax, keep=("left",), grid=None); ax.set_xticks([])
mv.titles(fig, headline, subtitle); mv.source(fig, source)
mv.lint(fig)   # checks colors, zero baseline, labels vs. axis
HTML

Copy templates/html/chart-card.html: headline, subtitle and source are HTML, colors come from CSS variables such as var(--mck-chart-focus), and the chart is drawn after the font loads.

R

source("dist/r/theme_mck.R"), then geom_col(aes(fill = job_family), width = 0.67) + scale_fill_manual(values = mck_highlight(levels(df$job_family), focus = focus), guide = "none") + theme_mck().

Coding agents

"Make a McKesson bar chart of voluntary attrition by job family, FY26, highlighting the families above the enterprise rate." The mck-chart skill runs the workflow and returns the chart, a chart brief and alt text.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideMagnitude19

Part-to-whole

Stacked bar chart

Part-to-whole charts show how a whole breaks into its parts, and how each part relates to the total.

A 100% stacked bar compares the mix of several wholes at once. Color only the segment the headline is about, and put it on the baseline or at the end of each bar.

McKesson spec

  • Five segments at most; group the rest as "Other"
  • White separators between segments
  • Labels inside segments that fit; key top-left in stack order
  • Sort the bars by the segment that matters
  1. 1Insight headlineNames the part and how far it stands out.
  2. 2SubtitleMetric, unit, scope, period.
  3. 3The part that mattersOne segment in blue, at the end of every bar.
  4. 4Grey contextTwo greys for the other parts.
  5. 5Labels in the segmentsWhere they fit; navy on grey, white on blue.
  6. 6Key in stack orderTop-left, left to right as the segments run.
  7. 7Echo the valueThe story segment's value at the bar end, bold for the focus bar.
  8. 8Sorted by the storyBars ordered by the blue segment, not alphabetically.
  9. 9Footnote and sourceDefine the parts.
McKesson Data Visualization GuidePart-to-whole20

Part-to-whole

Stacked bar variants

Same rules: one part in color, the rest grey, labels in place.

When a stack is the wrong chart

  • One whole with up to five parts: a donut or a single bar
  • How a total changes step by step: a waterfall
  • Many parts or a hierarchy: a treemap
  • Comparing the parts themselves across groups: grouped bars or small multiples; only the baseline segment of a stack compares cleanly

Stacked columns with totals

When the total matters too. The FY30 Data & AI gap of 617 FTE: reskilling (on the baseline) closes 40%.

Diverging stacked bars

Survey scales. Unfavorable in orange left of zero (it means worse), favorable in blue, neutral split across the middle.

Marimekko

Width and height both carry data: column width is each function's workforce, height its mix. Powerful, but it needs explaining.

Mix over time

A few periods as 100% columns, the tracked segment on the baseline so its change reads directly.

McKesson Data Visualization GuidePart-to-whole21

Part-to-whole

Stacked bar best practice

Stacks are easy to make and easy to misread. Four rules keep them honest.

The part that matters on the baseline. Only segments that share a starting line can be compared by eye.

Five segments at most. More slices turn a bar into a barcode. Keep the parts the story needs and group the rest.

Label in place; key in stack order. If a key is needed, put it top-left, in the same order as the segments.

One order in every bar. Never re-sort segments within each bar.

The part that matters on the baseline

✕Try to avoidA floating segment can't be compared across bars.
✓RecommendedOn the baseline, every bar starts level.

Five segments at most

✕Try to avoidEight colored slices nobody can follow.
✓RecommendedThe part in blue, the rest in grey.

Label in place, key in order

✕Try to avoidA bottom legend in a different order.
✓RecommendedValues inside, key top-left in stack order.

One order in every bar

✕Try to avoidSegments re-sorted inside each bar.
✓RecommendedThe same order everywhere.
McKesson Data Visualization GuidePart-to-whole22

Part-to-whole

Waterfall chart

A waterfall shows how a starting total becomes an ending total, one driver at a time.

It is a stacked column chart with an invisible spacer series that floats each driver at the running total. Use it for labor cost bridges, headcount bridges and budget-to-actual walks.

McKesson spec

  • Totals in navy; drivers grey; the drivers the headline names in blue
  • Thin light connectors between bars
  • Signed labels on drivers (true minus, explicit +); bold totals
  • If the axis starts above zero, mark the break and say so
  1. 1Insight headlineSizes what the named drivers did to the total.
  2. 2SubtitleFrom and to, with the unit.
  3. 3Totals in navyStart, end and any subtotal.
  4. 4Marked breakThe axis starts at $3,900M; white slashes say so.
  5. 5The drivers that matterIn blue; label bold.
  6. 6Thin connectorsLight grey, so the bars stay dominant.
  7. 7Signed labels+139, −58: direction without color.
  8. 8Grey contextEvery other driver, in logical order.
  9. 9FootnoteStates the axis break.
McKesson Data Visualization GuidePart-to-whole23

Part-to-whole

Waterfall variants

The same build, turned or recolored for the job.

Color by direction only when direction is the point. In a headcount bridge, additions in blue and losses in orange read instantly, because orange means "worse". In a cost bridge the default stays grey with a blue highlight.

Excel's built-in Waterfall chart is vertical only. For horizontal waterfalls or per-bar colors, build a stacked bar with a transparent spacer series (see the cookbook).

Horizontal waterfall

Long driver names, narrow layouts and phones.

Colored by direction

Frontline headcount bridge: voluntary exits equal 97% of external hires.

With a subtotal

A light-blue subtotal separates cost growth from the savings that offset it.

Distribution waterfall

Contributions to one total instead of steps in time: data engineering is 34% of the FY30 gap.

McKesson Data Visualization GuidePart-to-whole24

Part-to-whole

Waterfall best practice

The bars carry the story; everything else stays quiet.

Thin connectors. Heavy dark connectors compete with the bars. Use hairlines in light grey.

No red and green. They fail for color-blind readers and aren't McKesson colors. Grey drivers with a blue highlight, or blue and orange when direction is the story.

Mark a broken axis. Totals often dwarf the drivers. Starting the axis above zero is allowed here, and only here, if the break is drawn and footnoted.

Group the small steps. Keep the drivers the story needs; fold the rest together.

Connector lines

✕Try to avoidHeavy, dark connectors.
✓RecommendedThin, light grey.

Coloring the bars

✕Try to avoidGreen up, red down.
✓RecommendedGrey drivers; the named ones blue.

A broken axis

✕Try to avoidCut totals with no warning.
✓RecommendedBreak marks and a note.

Group the small steps

✕Try to avoidTen narrow drivers to decode.
✓RecommendedFive steps, savings combined.
McKesson Data Visualization GuidePart-to-whole25

Part-to-whole

Treemap

Nested rectangles whose area is proportional to value. A treemap shows many parts, or a hierarchy, in one compact block.

Use it when there are too many parts for a donut or a stack (ten to thirty roles, sites or skills) and the point is which few dominate.

Don't use it when readers need to compare similar sizes precisely, or there are only a handful of parts: a sorted bar is clearer.

McKesson spec

  • Squarified layout, largest top-left
  • Thin, even white gutters
  • Grey tiles; the ones the headline names in blue
  • Name and value inside each tile that fits
  1. 1Insight headlineShare of the whole held by the named few.
  2. 2SubtitleWhat area measures, with the unit.
  3. 3Focus in blueThe two roles the headline names.
  4. 4Grey contextEvery other role, the same grey.
  5. 5Smallest lastBottom-right. Tiles too small for a label get none; list them in a footnote if they matter.
  6. 6Largest firstTop-left, flowing to the smallest; labels top-left inside each tile.
  7. 7Footnote and sourceDefine the measure.
McKesson Data Visualization GuidePart-to-whole26

Part-to-whole

Treemap best practice

A treemap works when it reads as one shape that flows from large to small.

Largest to smallest. Don't arrange tiles alphabetically or by an org grouping that breaks the flow.

Labels inside. No label bands or boxes over the tiles; they distort the areas. If a tile can't hold its label, leave it unlabelled or label it outside.

Even padding. Uneven gaps make similar tiles look different.

Few parts? Use a bar. Areas are harder to compare than lengths.

Arrange by size

✕Try to avoidAlphabetical strips.
✓RecommendedLargest top-left.

Labelling

✕Try to avoidLabel bands over the tiles.
✓RecommendedInside, top-left.

Padding

✕Try to avoidUneven gaps.
✓RecommendedThin, even gutters.

Few parts

✕Try to avoidFour similar tiles.
✓RecommendedA sorted bar ranks them.
McKesson Data Visualization GuidePart-to-whole27

Part-to-whole

Donut and pie

A donut shows one whole split into a few parts. Prefer it to a pie: readers follow the arc length around the ring, and the center holds the total.

Use it for one whole and at most five parts. To compare several wholes, use 100% stacked bars; for more parts, a bar or treemap.

McKesson spec

  • Five segments at most; "Other" last
  • Largest first, clockwise from 12 o'clock
  • Hole about 60% of the diameter; white separators
  • Labels and values outside; no legend
  1. 1Insight headlineThe share, and what it means for the plan.
  2. 2SubtitleThe whole, the unit, the year.
  3. 3Start at 12Largest first, then clockwise.
  4. 4The part that mattersIn blue; the rest grey.
  5. 5Total in the centerLight weight, large.
  6. 6Labels outsideName and share, beside each segment.
  7. 7White separatorsThin gaps keep segments distinct.
  8. 8Footnote and sourceDefine the parts.
McKesson Data Visualization GuidePart-to-whole28

Part-to-whole

Donut best practice

People judge length faster than angle or area, which is why the donut beats the pie.

Donut over pie. The ring turns angles into arc lengths, and the hole holds the total.

Labels outside. Squeezed labels on the ring are hard to read; put names and values outside.

Few segments. Group the smallest into "Other".

Largest first, clockwise from 12. Don't mix small and large at random.

Progress rings and dials for a single percentage are in Single number.

Donut over pie

✕Try to avoidAngles and areas.
✓RecommendedArc lengths on a ring.

Labelling

✕Try to avoidLabels squeezed onto the ring.
✓RecommendedOutside, with the share.

Many small segments

✕Try to avoidNine slices, nine colors.
✓RecommendedThe story, plus "Other".

Order of segments

✕Try to avoidNo order, odd start.
✓RecommendedLargest first from 12.
McKesson Data Visualization GuidePart-to-whole29

Part-to-whole

Build part-to-whole charts

Every tool can make these natively. The settings below are the ones that matter; tested code and click-by-click steps are on the cookbook pages.

stacked-bar.md · waterfall.md · treemap.md · donut-pie.md

Before you send it

  • Parts sum to the whole (100%, or the end total)
  • Five parts at most; "Other" last
  • One part in color, matching the headline
  • Waterfall axis break marked and footnoted
  • No group under 10 people, in any part
PowerPoint and Excel

Stacked: Stacked or 100% Stacked Bar, Gap Width 50%, Overlap 100%, white 1.5 pt borders; move the story series first or last in Select Data. Waterfall: Insert › Waterfall, then right-click each total › Set as Total; drivers grey, totals navy. Treemap: Insert › Hierarchy › Treemap; labels Overlapping, not Banner. Donut: Doughnut, angle of first slice 0°, hole 62%, data sorted descending.

Power BI

Native 100% stacked bar, Waterfall, Treemap and Donut visuals all take the theme. Set the story color per series or with a field-value color measure; legend top-left or off; data labels on. The native waterfall can't color single bars or break the axis: use a stacked column with a transparent spacer measure when you need that.

Python

ax.barh(..., left=running_total, edgecolor="white") for stacks; the waterfall, squarified treemap and donut recipes in the cookbook use only matplotlib and mckviz. Plotly has native go.Waterfall, go.Treemap and go.Pie(hole=0.6).

colors = mv.highlight(parts, focus="Contingent")          # one part blue, rest grey
mv.lint(fig)    # flags > 6 colors, legends, and bars that don't start at zero
HTML

Plotly with MCK_PLOTLY_TEMPLATE: barmode: "stack", waterfall and treemap traces. Read colors from var(--mck-chart-focus) and var(--mck-chart-context).

R

geom_col(position = "fill") for 100% stacks; treemapify::geom_treemap() for treemaps; waterfalls with geom_rect(). Colors from mck_highlight().

McKesson Data Visualization GuidePart-to-whole30

Change over time

Line chart

Change-over-time charts show how something moves, and when it changed, at any time scale from weeks to decades.

A line connects values at equal time intervals, so the eye reads the trend rather than the individual amounts. Use it for monthly or quarterly attrition, hiring velocity, or a forecast.

McKesson spec

  • The series the headline names in blue; others grey
  • Data lines about twice the gridline weight
  • Names at the line ends, not in a legend
  • Shade the period that explains the change
  1. 1Insight headlineWhat changed, by how much, and why.
  2. 2SubtitleMetric, unit, scope and period.
  3. 3Focus lineBlue and heavier than the rest.
  4. 4Context linesGrey and thinner: there to compare against.
  5. 5The period that mattersLightly shaded and named.
  6. 6Direct labelsNames and latest values at the line ends, nudged apart.
  7. 7The change, sizedA short callout carries the headline number.
  8. 8Light scaffoldingA few thin gridlines; the unit lives in the subtitle.
  9. 9Footnote and sourceDefine the metric.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideChange over time31

Change over time

Line chart variants

The same rules hold: one line in blue, names at the ends, light scaffolding.

When a line is the wrong chart

  • Only two to five periods, and the amounts matter: columns
  • How a total splits over time: stacked area
  • Discrete events of different sizes: a bubble timeline
  • Many series that tangle: small multiples
  • Two measures in different units: two aligned charts, never a dual axis

Forecast with a range

Dashed beyond the last actual, inside a band that widens with time. Label it as an estimate.

Indexed to 100

Compares growth when the units or sizes differ: market Data & AI postings reached 196, our headcount 122.

Few points, every value labelled

With five annual values, label each one and drop the axis.

Sparklines

One small line per row in a table or dashboard: shape, latest value, change. Worse in orange-brown.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideChange over time32

Change over time

Line chart best practice

Four rules that make trends readable.

Highlight one line. A color per series doesn't show the trend; it makes the reader decode. Grey the background, color the message.

Lines for trends. Stacked columns hide how each part changes. When the trend is the point, draw lines.

No fill without a zero. Shading under a line turns it into an area chart, which implies a zero baseline.

Names at the line ends. A legend above the chart breaks the reading order.

Highlights

✕Try to avoidEvery line its own color.
✓RecommendedGrey context, one blue line.

Showing trends

✕Try to avoidStacks hide each part's change.
✓RecommendedLines show the crossover.

Shading lines

✕Try to avoidA filled area on a 20–36 axis.
✓RecommendedA plain line.

Labelling lines

✕Try to avoidA legend to decode.
✓RecommendedNames where the lines end.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideChange over time33

Change over time

Line chart best practice, continued

Four more, from HR and workforce data in particular.

Honest time spacing. Missing years still take up space. Use a real date axis, not evenly spaced labels.

Show gaps as gaps. A system change or survey break is not a straight line. Leave the gap and say why.

Weight with intent. Data lines about twice the gridlines; gridlines light, or gone.

Too many lines? Split them. More than four or five crossing lines become spaghetti. Use small multiples.

Even time intervals

✕Try to avoidMissing years squeezed out.
✓RecommendedTrue spacing; the slope is honest.

Missing data

✕Try to avoidDrawing across the gap.
✓RecommendedA visible, labelled gap.

Line weight

✕Try to avoidGridlines outweigh the data.
✓RecommendedData lines twice the grid.

Too many lines

✕Try to avoidSix crossing colors.
✓RecommendedSmall multiples.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideChange over time34

Change over time

Stacked area chart

Layers stacked on each other show how a total splits over time, and how each part's share shifts.

Use it for a few parts that change gradually: how a role's hours divide between activities, or how the workforce mix moves. The layer on the baseline is the only one that reads precisely, so put the story there.

McKesson spec

  • Four or five layers at most
  • The story layer on the baseline, in blue; the rest ordered greys
  • Labels inside or at the right edge, not in a legend
  • Mark the event that explains the shift
  1. 1Insight headlineStart, end and the reason.
  2. 2SubtitleWhose time, what unit, which years.
  3. 3Story on the baselineBlue, so its growth reads directly.
  4. 4Grey contextOrdered from dark to light.
  5. 5Labels at the endName and latest share beside each layer.
  6. 6The event, markedA thin dashed line and a short name.
  7. 7Where it startedThe first value, so the change is explicit.
  8. 8Footnote and sourceHow time was measured.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideChange over time35

Change over time

Stacked area best practice

Areas are heavy marks. Keep them few, ordered and calm.

Stack, don't overlap. Areas drawn over each other hide what's behind. Stack them, or use lines.

Order the colors. Random colors make neighbors clash. Story layer blue on the baseline; the rest in ordered greys.

Volatile on top. A jumpy layer at the bottom makes every layer above it jump. Keep steady layers low.

Few layers. Four or five at most; fold the rest into "Other".

Overlapping areas

✕Try to avoidTranslucent layers over each other.
✓RecommendedStacked layers.

Color order

✕Try to avoidUnrelated bright colors.
✓RecommendedBlue story, ordered greys.

High variability

✕Try to avoidThe volatile layer at the bottom.
✓RecommendedSteady layers low, volatile on top.

Number of layers

✕Try to avoidNine thin layers.
✓RecommendedThree: story, comparison, rest.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideChange over time36

Change over time

Bubble timeline

Events placed on a time axis, with bubble area showing size. It combines a timeline with a proportional-area chart.

Use it for discrete events of different sizes: announced layoffs in the talent market, reorganizations, hiring waves. Each category gets its own row.

McKesson spec

  • Bubble area, not diameter, proportional to value
  • One grey for all rows; the headline's row in blue
  • Largest bubbles drawn first, with white outlines
  • A size key with two or three reference circles
  1. 1Insight headlineWho stands out, by how much.
  2. 2SubtitleSays what bubble area means.
  3. 3One row per categorySorted by total, largest on top.
  4. 4Time along the bottomEven intervals, years labelled.
  5. 5Size keyReference circles; area ∝ value.
  6. 6Focus rowBlue; white outlines keep overlaps readable.
  7. 7The period that mattersShaded and named.
  8. 8Footnote and sourceWhat counts as an event.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideChange over time37

Change over time

Bubble timeline best practice

The rows already separate the categories; let size do the rest.

One color. Coloring each row repeats what the rows already say. Use grey, and blue for the headline's row.

Don't hide small bubbles. Draw the largest first, with white outlines.

Sort the rows. By total, or by a meaningful order, not alphabetically.

Show the scale. Without a size key, readers can only say "bigger".

Coloring bubbles

✕Try to avoidA color per row.
✓RecommendedGrey, one row blue.

Overlapping bubbles

✕Try to avoidBig bubbles on top.
✓RecommendedBig behind, white outlines.

Row order

✕Try to avoidAlphabetical rows.
✓RecommendedSorted by total.

Size key

✕Try to avoidNo way to read size.
✓RecommendedTwo reference circles.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideChange over time38

Change over time

Small multiples

The same small chart repeated for each group, on one shared scale. The eye compares shapes across panels instead of untangling crossing lines.

Use it when six or more groups each need their own trend: business units, regions, job families. In each panel, the panel's own line is blue and the others sit faintly behind it.

McKesson spec

  • One shared scale, stated once
  • Panels ordered by value or a natural order
  • Panel title = name + latest value
  • Axis labels only on the outer edge
  1. 1Insight headlineThe one panel that differs.
  2. 2SubtitleMetric, unit, period, once for all panels.
  3. 3The exceptionIn orange, because it is getting worse.
  4. 4Its own line in blueThe other units faint behind it, for context.
  5. 5Ordered by valueHighest latest value first.
  6. 6Shared scale0–12% in every panel.
  7. 7Title carries the numberName and latest value.
  8. 8Outer axes onlyLabels on the left column and bottom row.
  9. 9Footnote and sourceDefine the metric.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideChange over time39

Change over time

Small multiples best practice

Small multiples only work if every panel is read the same way.

One scale. Independent scales make a 0.5-point wobble look like the 5-point rise.

Context in every panel. The other units, faint behind each line, show whether a panel is unusual.

Order with meaning. By value, size or geography, not the alphabet.

Label the edges only. Repeated axes are clutter the eye reads six times.

Shared scale

✕Try to avoidEvery panel zooms itself.
✓RecommendedOne scale; the rise stands out.

Context

✕Try to avoidLines alone.
✓RecommendedThe others faint behind.

Panel order

✕Try to avoidAlphabetical.
✓RecommendedBy latest value.

Axes

✕Try to avoidAxes on every panel.
✓RecommendedOuter edge only.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideChange over time40

Change over time

Build change-over-time charts

Native, editable charts in every tool. Tested code and click-by-click steps are on the cookbook pages.

line.md · stacked-area.md · bubble-timeline.md · small-multiples.md

Before you send it

  • Time left to right, at true intervals
  • One line or layer in blue, matching the headline
  • Names at line ends; no legend
  • Forecasts dashed, labelled and with a range
  • Small multiples share one scale
PowerPoint and Excel

Line: Insert › Line; format the focus series 2.25 pt Focus blue, the rest 1.25 pt grey; delete the legend and add data labels to the last point only (Series Name + Value). Use a date axis so missing periods keep their space. Stacked area: Insert › 100% Stacked Area; story series first in Select Data; white 1 pt borders. Small multiples: build one chart, fix the axis bounds (Minimum/Maximum, not Auto), then copy it per group.

Power BI

Line chart with the focus series colored by measure; turn off the legend and use Series labels. Forecast bands as low/high measures shown with Error bars › Shaded area. Small multiples are built in: add the group to Small multiples and keep Y-axis › Shared.

Python

matplotlib with mckviz; mv.label_line_ends(ax) places and nudges end labels; mv.shade_period(ax, start, end, label) marks the period.

for fam, s in df.items():                 # one column per job family, one row per quarter
    ax.plot(x, s, label=fam, color=C.focus if fam == focus else C.context,
            lw=2.4 if fam == focus else 1.4)
mv.shade_period(ax, 6, 11, "After the reset")
mv.label_line_ends(ax, fmt="{:.1f}")      # names at the ends, nudged apart
HTML

Plotly scatter traces with mode: "lines", an annotation per line end, and a shape for the shaded period; facet_col (Plotly Express) for small multiples with shared axes.

R

geom_line() with mck_highlight() colors and geom_text() end labels; geom_area() for stacks; facet_wrap(~ unit) keeps a shared scale by default.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideChange over time41

Geo-spatial

Choropleth map

Geo-spatial charts show where: a pattern across geography, or values at precise locations.

A choropleth shades each area by a rate: postings per candidate, attrition, share eligible to retire. Use it when the pattern only makes sense on a map.

Real shapes let big, empty states dominate. A tile grid gives each state one equal square in roughly its place.

McKesson spec

  • Sequential blue in 3–5 even classes
  • Light base, thin white boundaries
  • Label only the areas the headline names
  1. 1Insight headlineNames the states and the threshold.
  2. 2SubtitleA rate, with its unit, scope and period.
  3. 3One tile per stateEqual size, in roughly its place.
  4. 4Classed keyFive even classes, open-ended, high on top.
  5. 5Values on the fewOnly the 1.7+ states carry a number.
  6. 6Callout on the outlierA ring and a two-line note.
  7. 7Quiet structureThin white gutters, small abbreviations.
  8. 8Footnote and sourceDefine the rate; say it's a tile map.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideGeo-spatial42

Geo-spatial

Bubble map

Bubbles on a quiet base map show counts at locations: headcount by site, open requisitions by metro, hires by campus.

Bubble area carries the count. Color can carry a second measure with the focus rule: blue for the sites the headline names, grey for the rest.

McKesson spec

  • Area ∝ value; largest drawn first, white outlines
  • Largest bubble about 40–56 px across
  • Label the focus sites: bold value, then name
  • Drop sites under 10 people and footnote them
  1. 1Insight headlineThe sites, the threshold, what's at stake.
  2. 2SubtitleSays what area and color mean.
  3. 3Area = associatesScaled by area, never radius.
  4. 4Focus in blueThe sites at 12%+ vacancy.
  5. 5Direct labelsBold value and site name, for the focus only.
  6. 6Grey contextEvery other site; overlaps stay readable.
  7. 7Size and color keyTwo reference circles, two swatches.
  8. 8Quiet baseSand tiles, no borders: the map is context.
  9. 9Footnote and sourceDefine vacancy; note what's suppressed.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideGeo-spatial43

Geo-spatial

Map variants

Same base, same quiet structure; the variant follows the question.

When a map is the wrong chart

  • Readers need to rank or compare precisely: a sorted bar
  • Five locations or fewer: a bar or a table
  • Change over time in each region: small multiples of lines
  • Geography is only a grouping (business units, divisions): no map at all

Diverging classes

When a midpoint means something. Technician pay is 6%+ below market in three states, all of them among the tightest.

Dot density

Spread and concentration. 63% of remote Customer Care agents live outside the three hub states.

Small-multiple maps

Two periods on the same classes: 1 state at 1.7+ in 2024, 4 in 2026.

Map plus ranked bar

The map shows where; the bar shows by how much. Same blue for the same states.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideGeo-spatial44

Geo-spatial

Maps best practice

Maps are persuasive, so they must be honest about what the color means.

Rates, not counts. Shading headcount or postings just redraws where people live. Normalize: per candidate, per 1,000, a %. Show counts as bubbles.

Even, round classes. Three to five, no gaps or overlaps, open-ended at both ends.

One sequential hue. A rainbow makes some hues pop for no reason. Diverging only around a meaningful midpoint.

A quiet base. Light sand, thin white boundaries. For print, darken them to grey.

Rates, not counts

✕Try to avoidRaw postings: big states win.
✓RecommendedPostings per candidate.

Class breaks

✕Try to avoidUneven, gappy, overlapping.
✓RecommendedFive even, round classes.

Color scale

✕Try to avoidRainbow, off palette.
✓RecommendedLight to dark blue.

Base map

✕Try to avoidA dark base competes.
✓RecommendedSand base, data on top.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideGeo-spatial45

Geo-spatial

Maps best practice, continued

Four more, from workforce data in particular.

Bubbles by area. Scaling the radius makes a site twice as big look four times as big.

Label the few that matter. A number in every state is a table in the wrong shape.

Is it really geographic? Three hubs don't need a map of fifty states.

Aggregate, then map. Never plot home addresses. Map to state, metro or site, and drop anything under 10 people, in tooltips too.

Bubble size

✕Try to avoidRadius ∝ value.
✓RecommendedArea ∝ value.

Labels

✕Try to avoidA value in every state.
✓RecommendedOnly the four named.

Is it geographic?

✕Try to avoidA US map for three sites.
✓RecommendedA sorted bar.

Protect people

✕Try to avoidExact spots; a site of 7.
✓RecommendedAggregated; small sites dropped.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideGeo-spatial46

Geo-spatial

Build maps

Choropleths are native in every tool; bubble and dot maps are easiest in Python or Plotly. Tested code and click-by-click steps are on the cookbook page.

maps.md

Before you send it

  • Shaded values are rates; counts are bubbles
  • 3–5 even classes; the key names the unit
  • Equal-area projection or tile grid
  • Only the named areas or sites labelled
  • No area, site or cluster under 10 people
PowerPoint and Excel

Choropleth: Insert › Charts › Maps › Filled Map (online: Excel geocodes through Bing). Format Data Series: Map projection Albers, Map area Only regions with data, Map labels None. Excel only draws continuous scales, so map a class-number column (1–5) to get binned shades, and draw the key as five small squares. Delete the title and legend; label the focus states with text boxes. Bubble and dot maps aren't native: build them in Python and insert the SVG.

Power BI

Azure Maps visual (your admin must enable it): Filled map layer for rates; Bubble layer with Range scaling Magnitude for counts. Bin colors with a SWITCH measure in Fill color › fx › Field value. Suppress small groups with IF([Headcount] < 10, BLANK(), ...), and check geocoding against data-handling rules.

Python

The tile grid needs only matplotlib and mckviz. For real shapes, Plotly go.Choropleth(locationmode="USA-states") and go.Scattergeo(scope="usa") use Albers USA.

cls = pd.cut(rate, [-np.inf, 0.8, 1.1, 1.4, 1.7, np.inf], labels=False, right=False)
ramp = [mv.SEQUENTIAL["blue"][i] for i in (0, 1, 2, 4, 5)]
marker={"size": n, "sizemode": "area", "color": mv.pl_highlight(sites, focus=hot)}
HTML

Plotly with MCK_PLOTLY_TEMPLATE; headline, subtitle and source in the chart card's HTML. Tooltips may show n, but never for an area or site under 10.

R

geom_polygon() on map_data("state") with coord_map("albers", lat0 = 29.5, lat1 = 45.5) and scale_fill_manual() on the classes; bubbles with scale_size_area().

McKesson Data Visualization GuideGeo-spatial47

Single number

Big number and KPI card

Single-number charts make one value the message, with the context and comparison that give it meaning.

Use a big number when one value is the finding: an executive summary, a slide opener, a report margin, the header row of a dashboard.

McKesson spec

  • Numeral Light 300, navy; never bold
  • One sentence on exactly what is counted
  • Always a comparison; "pts" for point changes
  • Source and as-of date on the card itself
  1. 1Insight headlineThe movement and the gap that remains.
  2. 2SubtitleMetric, scope, date and the base.
  3. 3The numberLarge, Light weight, rounded hard.
  4. 4One sentenceCounts make the % concrete.
  5. 5ComparisonSigned, in pts, teal and ▲ because it's good news.
  6. 6Gap to targetOrange text because it's worse, said in words.
  7. 7Progress bar0–100% track, target tick labelled.
  8. 8Footnote and sourceDefine the measure; date it.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideSingle number48

Single number

Progress ring

A ring shows one share of one whole moving toward a target: skills profiles completed, required learning done, plan positions filled.

It works only on a 0–100% scale. If the value can pass 100% or go negative, show the big number and the delta instead.

McKesson spec

  • Starts at 12 o'clock, runs clockwise
  • Blue arc, sand remainder; hole about 80%
  • No rounded caps, gaps, gradients or 3D
  • Target as a thin tick, labelled
  1. 1Insight headlineWhere we are and how far to go.
  2. 2SubtitleMetric, date and the base.
  3. 3Start at 12Then clockwise, like a clock.
  4. 4Blue arc, sand trackThe remainder stays visible.
  5. 5Number in the centerLight weight; the only centered text.
  6. 6Target tickThin, navy, named.
  7. 7Thin strokeAbout 18% of the radius.
  8. 8Sentence and comparisonLeft-aligned beside the ring.
  9. 9Footnote and sourceWhat "verified" means.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideSingle number49

Single number

Single number variants

The anatomy stays the same: name, number, comparison, sentence.

When a single number is the wrong chart

  • The trend is the message: a line, or a sparkline under the number
  • Many groups to compare: bars; eight KPI cards are a bar chart in disguise
  • Several parts of a whole: a donut or stacked bar
  • The base is under 10 people: don't headline it

Big number with a trend

A sparkline adds the shape without a full chart: internal fill reached 29%, +5 pts in a year.

Progress bars to a target

One share per group on a shared 0–100% track. 5 of 6 units are below target; Oncology is lowest at 44%.

Circular dials

One % across a few groups, every ring 0–100%. Distribution trails at 61%.

KPI row

Three to five cards above a dashboard's main chart, each built the same way. Days to fill rose 2 days, so it's orange.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideSingle number50

Single number

Single number best practice

A number alone is a fact. Context and comparison make it a finding.

Light, large, plain. The numeral needs size and space, not bold type, boxes or shadows.

Say what is counted. One sentence, with the base: "254 of 410 critical roles".

Always compare. Prior period, target or benchmark, with a sign. Percentage-point changes are "pts", never "%".

No speedometers. Gauges spend ink on a dial and invite red and green. A ring or a bar with a target does the job.

Light, large, plain

✕Try to avoidBold, boxed, shadowed.
✓RecommendedLight numeral, white space.

Say what is counted

✕Try to avoid62% of what?
✓RecommendedOne sentence with the base.

Always compare

✕Try to avoid"+14%" against nothing.
✓RecommendedPts vs. a date; gap to target.

No speedometers

✕Try to avoidDial, needle, traffic lights.
✓RecommendedA thin ring with a target.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideSingle number51

Single number

Single number best practice, continued

Four more, from dashboards and scorecards.

Color by judgment, not direction. Teal when the change is good, orange when it's worse. Days to fill going up is bad news; pair the color with ▲▼ or words.

Round hard. 62%, 4.3K, $1.2M. Decimals suggest a precision the data doesn't have.

Rings are for 0–100%. Growth, indexes and variances get a big number and a delta.

One anatomy per row. Same order, weight and alignment in every card.

Color by judgment

✕Try to avoidUp = green, whatever it means.
✓RecommendedTeal good, orange worse.

Round hard

✕Try to avoidFalse precision.
✓RecommendedWhole points.

Rings are for 0–100%

✕Try to avoidA ring that laps itself.
✓RecommendedBig number, with a benchmark.

One anatomy per row

✕Try to avoidEvery card different.
✓RecommendedName, number, change.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideSingle number52

Single number

Build a KPI card

A big number is type, not a chart: build it from text wherever you can, so it stays sharp and editable.

kpi-big-number.md

Before you send it

  • Number, sentence and headline agree (62% × 410 ≈ 254)
  • A comparison with a sign; "pts" for points
  • Colors by favorability, plus ▲▼ or words
  • Rings only for 0–100% of one whole
  • No KPI based on fewer than 10 people
PowerPoint and Excel

Big number: a text box in Libre Franklin Light, 54 pt, Navy #143359, left inset 0; the sentence below at 14 pt; the comparison in Medium, teal #00737A or orange #A75B00. Align left and group. Ring: a Doughnut of value and remainder, Angle of first slice 0°, Hole Size 80%, fills #005A8C / #DEDBD1, no borders, title, legend or labels; lay the number over the center.

Power BI

Card (new): the measure as the callout value (raise it to 40–54; Segoe UI Light in the service), Reference labels for the comparison. The KPI visual adds trend and target: set Good #00AF9D, Bad #EF8200 and the direction per metric. Rings: a Donut with Inner radius ≈ 80 and a transparent Card on top.

Python

matplotlib Wedge for the ring; Plotly go.Indicator(mode="number+delta") for a KPI row, with increasing / decreasing colors set by favorability.

KPI = mv.TOKENS["typography"]["roles"]["kpi"]        # Light 300
ax.text(0, 0, f"{value}%", fontsize=KPI["size_pt"] * 0.75,
        fontweight=KPI["weight"], color=C.headline)
txt = f"{mv.signed(value - prior)} pts vs. Mar 2025"   # true minus, explicit +
HTML

Plain HTML text beats a chart library here: <p class="mck-kpi"> from mck-viz.css sets --mck-kpi-size (56 px) and --mck-kpi-weight (300). Color deltas with var(--mck-semantic-positive-text) and var(--mck-semantic-negative-text).

R

annotate("text", ..., family = "Libre Franklin Light") for the number; a ring with geom_col() + coord_polar(theta = "y", start = 0, direction = 1).

McKesson Data Visualization GuideSingle number53

Formats

Presentations: build it up

The same data needs different treatment on a live slide, a page, a phone or a dashboard. Design for where it will be seen.

In a live meeting, don't reveal a finished chart in one click. Build it in two to five steps so the audience learns the chart before you give them the point.

1 Set the scene. Axes, labels and the data, all grey.

2 Highlight the insight. Color what the headline names.

3 Show the full picture. Add the benchmark and the callout.

Keep the headline, axis and order identical on every step; only the emphasis changes.

Step 1 · Set the scene

Everything the reader needs to read the chart, nothing to interpret yet.

Step 2 · Highlight

The two families the headline names turn blue.

Step 3 · Full picture

Benchmark and callout: 73% of all voluntary exits.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideFormats54

Formats

Presentations: clarity first

A slide is on screen for less than a minute. There is no time to explore it.

  • The slide title is the headline
  • One message per chart; at most two charts per slide, never a chart wall
  • Short text beside the chart, or none
  • Native, editable charts from the starter deck, not pictures of charts
  • In a dimmed room, use the dark slide: navy background, light-blue focus

Chart wall

✕Try to avoidA label title, four charts and a column of bullets.

One message

✓RecommendedHeadline as title, one chart, a source line.

Dimmed room

✓RecommendedThe same slide on navy; focus in light blue.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideFormats55

Formats

Reports and print

On paper the reader sets the pace, so charts can carry more context: full footnotes, more categories, a second chart.

  • Fit the page grid: full page, two-column or one column
  • Export vector (PDF, SVG), or PNG at 300 dpi
  • Nothing below 9 pt; check the printed size, not the screen
  • Grey must survive a black-and-white printer: never rely on color alone

Featured

One chart takes a page, for the exhibit the report is built around.

Editorial

Charts sit in the two- or three-column grid next to the text that discusses them.

Inline

A small chart inside one text column drives home a single point.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideFormats56

Formats

Web and mobile

A phone is narrow and read at arm's length. Adapt the chart, don't just shrink it.

Resize and reorient. Design for portrait; columns become horizontal bars.

Adjust the hierarchy. When end labels don't fit, use a compact key above the chart and move the insight to the top.

Reduce complexity. One highlighted line, the rest faint; the insight next to it.

Ensure legibility. Fewer text elements, shorter headline, nothing below 11 px.

Phone

Test at 390 px

In HTML, the starter card (templates/html/chart-card.html) already swaps line-end labels for a top key below 600 px. Check every web chart at 390 px wide, the width of a typical phone, before it ships.

In Power BI, build a separate mobile layout for each page people will open on a phone.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideFormats57

Formats

Dashboards (Power BI and Fabric)

Dashboards are exploratory, but the same rules apply: grey context, one blue focus, insight titles, minimum group sizes.

  • One question per page; the title states the current answer (a DAX measure can write it)
  • KPI cards top-left: the number, its label, and the comparison
  • Highlights driven by measures, not by clicking bars
  • Minimum n enforced in the measures, so tooltips and drill-throughs inherit it
  • No gauges, pies of many slices, or rainbow defaults

Set-up: docs/powerbi-setup.md and the theme in dist/powerbi/.

Tool defaults

✕Try to avoidGauges, a rainbow pie and columns, a label title. Nothing says what matters.

Built to answer a question

✓RecommendedAn insight title, three KPI cards with comparisons, a highlighted bar and the trend.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideFormats58

Formats

Interactivity with a purpose

Interaction lets readers explore at their own pace, but every control must earn its place.

  • The default view tells the story without any clicks
  • Each interaction answers a question the reader will have
  • Tooltips add detail; they never carry the main point
  • Filters and tooltips respect the minimum group size

Cursor tracking

A rule and a tooltip follow the cursor on time series, where reading values off the axis is hard.

InteractionUse it for
HoverDetail on one mark: the value, n, definition
Cursor trackingExact values on line charts
Toggles and filtersSwitching series or groups on and off
SlidersScenario inputs in SWP models: attrition, hiring volume
Range selectionNarrowing time or values on an axis
ZoomDense time series
Play and scrubChange over time, when motion is the point
McKesson Data Visualization GuideFormats59

Formats

Animation and scrolly-telling

Motion should help the viewer follow the data, never decorate it.

Sequence on purpose. Axes first, then data, then the insight: the build order is the reading order.

Move naturally. Ease in and out; lines draw left to right; bubbles grow from their center. No overshoot or bounce.

Say what you see. Narration and text match what is moving on screen, one point at a time.

Scrolly-telling: the chart stays pinned and updates as the text scrolls. On phones use inline snapshots, and never hijack the scroll.

Frame 1

The frame: axes and labels.

Frame 2

Lines draw in from the left.

Frame 3

The gap shades in once both lines land.

Avoid motion without purpose. If nothing changes in the data, nothing should move.

Avoid distraction. One moving thing at a time; split complex charts into short sequences.

Exits mirror entrances. Leave the way you arrived, so the viewer can predict it.

McKesson Data Visualization GuideFormats60

Formats

Social, infographics and icons

Single-asset graphics are seen out of context, on a phone, in a second.

  • One insight, readable without zooming
  • Self-contained: headline, key number, source and brand mark
  • Three-tone palettes from the tokens: navy with white and light blue
  • Icons only when they help; if it's clear without one, leave it out

Use icons as tally units (one icon = a fixed number of people), never scaled up to show a bigger value.

Social card

Icons for quantities

✕Try to avoidDoubling the value doubles height and width: the icon looks four times bigger.
✓RecommendedRepeat a unit icon: 10 versus 20.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideFormats61

Toolkit

Set up once

Ten minutes per tool, and every chart you make afterwards starts on-brand.

Detailed steps, troubleshooting and screenshots:

  • docs/office-setup.md
  • docs/powerbi-setup.md
  • AGENTS.md (Python, HTML, R)
Fonts (everyone)

Install the Libre Franklin TTFs from fonts/LibreFranklin/ (right-click › Install for all users). Without them, Office and Power BI fall back to Arial or Segoe UI.

PowerPoint and Excel

Copy dist/office/Theme Colors/McKesson Data Viz.xml to %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Templates\Document Themes\Theme Colors\ and the Theme Fonts file to …\Theme Fonts\. Then Design › Variants › Colors / Fonts (PowerPoint) or Page Layout › Colors / Fonts (Excel). New decks start from McKesson-DataViz.potx.

Power BI

View › Themes › Browse for themes and pick dist/powerbi/mckesson-dataviz-theme.json. Viewers without Libre Franklin see Segoe UI, so leave room in labels.

Python
pip install -e ./python[examples]
import mckviz as mv
mv.use()          # fonts, matplotlib style, Plotly template "mck"
C = mv.colors     # C.focus, C.context, C.accent, C.negative ...
HTML

Link dist/web/mck-viz.css for the CSS variables and chart-card styles; add mck-plotly-template.js for Plotly or use vega-lite-config.json as the Vega-Lite config. Start from templates/html/chart-card.html.

R

source("dist/r/theme_mck.R"), then ff <- mck_font() and theme_mck(base_family = ff). Render with ragg.

Toolkit

Check before you send

Run this list on every chart that leaves the team, whoever or whatever made it.

In Python, mv.lint(fig) checks the mechanical items for you: titles and source present, at most six colors, palette only (amber is an error), no red–green, bars from zero, labels versus axis, legends, dual axes, pies, rotated or tiny text. It also reminds you to check any orange carries meaning.

No tool can tell whether the headline is true or the chart fits the question. That part needs a person, or an agent told to check.

Rendered from docs/qa-checklist.md, so it always matches.

Message

  • Headline is a full-sentence insight, ≤ 2 lines, no final period, balanced line breaks.
  • Every claim in the headline is visibly supported (recompute counts, multipliers, "all/most/none").
  • Subtitle states metric, unit, scope and period: and nothing opinionated.
  • The chart type matches the question (choosing-a-chart.md).
  • One message per chart; ≤ 2 charts per slide.

Color and emphasis

  • Highlight follows the headline: grey context, blue focus, navy accent: ≤ 2 highlighted items. Orange appears only where something is worse (negative, below target).
  • Categorical colors (if any) come from the fixed order, ≤ 6, consistent across the deck.
  • No red–green contrasts; nothing encoded by color alone.
  • Focus category labels are bolded/colored to echo the highlight.

Data integrity

  • Bars/columns start at zero (waterfall exception is marked and footnoted).
  • Bubble area ∝ value; pie/donut sums to 100% and has ≤ 5 segments.
  • No dual axes (or justified and clearly labelled).
  • Sorted by value, or in a natural order (time, bands, levels).
  • Small multiples share a scale.
  • Numbers rounded sensibly; units in subtitle; true minus (−); consistent K/M/B.

Clutter

  • Direct labels instead of a legend where possible; legend (if any) top-left, in data order.
  • No borders, 3D, shadows, gradients, heavy gridlines, tick marks, rotated axis titles.
  • Value axis removed when values are labelled.
  • Nothing overlaps: labels, callouts, legend, headline, reference lines.

Typography and layout

  • Libre Franklin (or approved fallback); role sizes per typography-and-layout.md; nothing below 9 pt / 11 px.
  • Headline, subtitle, key, footnote and source share one left edge.
  • Sentence case; consistent terminology (FTE vs. headcount; fiscal vs. calendar year).

Source and ethics

  • Footnotes define metrics and caveats.
  • Source line names the system(s), as-of date and population.
  • No group smaller than the minimum n (default 10): including in tooltips, filters and drill-downs.
  • Protected attributes used only for approved analyses, aggregated.
  • Forecasts/estimates are labelled and show a range or scenario.

Accessibility and delivery

  • Text contrast ≥ 4.5:1; fills < 3:1 carry labels.
  • Alt text / text summary provided (headline + key numbers).
  • Exported at the right format: native Office chart, SVG/PDF for print, PNG @ 300 dpi, or responsive HTML.
  • Mobile/dark variants checked if the chart will be shown that way.
McKesson Data Visualization GuideToolkit64

Toolkit

For coding agents

Claude, Copilot and other agents follow the same rules as people, automatically.

In this repo, agents read AGENTS.md on their own (Claude through CLAUDE.md, Copilot through .github/copilot-instructions.md, plus per-language rules for Python, web and R files).

In any other repo, copy one file: dist/agents/mck-viz-rules.md. It is generated from the tokens, so its colors are always current.

Ask for a chart like this

"Make a McKesson chart of voluntary attrition by job family for FY26 from attrition.csv, for a leadership deck. Highlight the families above the enterprise rate."

What comes back

The mck-chart skill walks the five steps (question, chart type, build, headline, QA), runs mv.lint, looks at the rendered chart, and returns the file, a chart brief and alt text.

The chart brief

Question:    Where is attrition concentrated?
Mode:        explanatory     Medium: slide
Chart:       sorted bar (cookbook/bar.md)
Focus:       2 families > enterprise rate
Headline:    Two frontline job families lose
             about 1 in 4 people a year ...
Subtitle:    Voluntary attrition by job
             family, FY26 (%)
Source:      Workday HCM, 31 Mar 2026
Min n check: smallest group 700 (>= 10)
QA:          pass
